headline: This file declares 2 spaces, 1 role declaration and 4 functions.

items.name: Small
summary: A value of `Small` is a list of 1000 numbers, where every position holds either +1 or -1, and two of them are combined by multiplying position against position. Nothing about that list means anything on its own; its meaning is which other values it was built from.

Several values can be added together into a single one, which is what `load` counts everywhere below. That only works up to a point. Past it, asking for one of the items back returns a different item instead, and nothing fails while it happens.
For `Small` that point is 31 items. It was measured at 95% retrieval, not derived from a formula.

items.name: Subject, Verb, Object
items.signature: role Subject, Verb, Object in Small
summary: Subject, Verb and Object are fixed values of `Small`, used as keys: attaching a value to one of them is how this program records which part that value plays.
Which keys a value carries is a compile-time fact, tracked through every operation, even though the values attached to them are not.

items.name: scene
items.signature: fn scene(s: Sym[Small], v: Sym[Small], o: Sym[Small]) -> Vec[Small; load 3]
summary: It takes three values, every one of them one single entry of `Small` — one of its fixed values, not a combination of several.
It gives back a value of `Small` whose keys the type does not pin down, holding 3 of the 31 items `Small` can hold.

facts.result_of_the_body: Vec[Small; load 3; roles {Subject, Verb, Object}; clean]

items.name: everything
items.signature: fn everything(a: Sym[Small], b: Sym[Small], c: Sym[Small], d: Sym[Small], e: Sym[Small], f: Sym[Small], g: Sym[Small], h: Sym[Small]) -> Vec[Small]
summary: It takes eight values, every one of them one single entry of `Small` — one of its fixed values, not a combination of several.
It gives back a value of `Small` whose keys the type does not pin down, holding at least 1 item.
notable: This is past capacity: 40 items in a space that holds 31. Some of what goes in cannot be got back out.

items.name: Sentences
summary: A value of `Sentences` is a list of 384 numbers, where every position holds either +1 or -1, and two of them are combined by multiplying position against position. Nothing about that list means anything on its own; its meaning is which other values it was built from.

Several values can be added together into a single one, which is what `load` counts everywhere below. That only works up to a point. Past it, asking for one of the items back returns a different item instead, and nothing fails while it happens.

For `Sentences` that point is 3 items. It was measured at 95% retrieval, not derived from a formula. That number comes from the measured effective width of 111 this declaration records, not from the 384 written beside the family: a real embedding space uses far fewer independent directions than its nominal width suggests.
notable: The written width would suggest room for 10 items. The measured width says 3. Anything sized against the written number is about 3x too optimistic.

items.name: pair
items.signature: fn pair(a: Sym[Sentences], b: Sym[Sentences]) -> Vec[Sentences; load 2]
summary: It takes two values, every one of them one single entry of `Sentences` — one of its fixed values, not a combination of several.
It gives back a value of `Sentences` whose keys the type does not pin down, holding 2 of the 3 items `Sentences` can hold.

items.name: quad
items.signature: fn quad(a: Sym[Sentences], b: Sym[Sentences], c: Sym[Sentences], d: Sym[Sentences]) -> Vec[Sentences]
summary: It takes four values, every one of them one single entry of `Sentences` — one of its fixed values, not a combination of several.
It gives back a value of `Sentences` whose keys the type does not pin down, holding at least 1 item.
notable: This is past capacity: 4 items in a space that holds 3. Some of what goes in cannot be got back out.
